questions.text: SSS and GSIS housing programs differ primarily in that SSS serves:

options.text: Government employees; GSIS serves the informal sector
Private sector workers; GSIS serves government employees
All employed workers regardless of sector; GSIS is limited to high-income earners
Voluntary members only; GSIS serves mandatory members

rationale.a: SSS serves private sector, not informal. GSIS serves government, not informal.
rationale.b: SSS is the Social Security System for private sector workers. GSIS (Government Service Insurance System) serves government employees. Both offer housing loans but to distinct beneficiary groups.
rationale.c: SSS is not universal employment; both have specific eligible groups.
rationale.d: Both SSS and GSIS are mandatory for their respective member classes.
rationale.correct: This question cannot be verified against the provided search results, which contain no information about SSS or GSIS housing programs. Recommend adding authoritative sources (SSS Charter, GSIS Charter) to the search results before using this question. Both offer housing loans but to distinct beneficiary groups.
rationale.takeaway: SSS = private sector workers; GSIS = government employees. Membership defines eligibility.

questions.text: Which of the following BEST distinguishes SHFC's Community Mortgage Program from Pag-IBIG's housing finance approach?

options.text: CMP is mandatory for all employees; Pag-IBIG is voluntary, which affects the participation rate.
CMP finances community organizations collectively; Pag-IBIG finances individual buyers
CMP is regulated by DHSUD; Pag-IBIG is regulated by NHA, which influences the regulatory framework.
CMP is available to government employees only; Pag-IBIG is for private sector workers, impacting eligibility.

rationale.a: Pag-IBIG is mandatory (payroll deduction); CMP membership is voluntary.
rationale.b: CMP's defining feature is community-level financing—the organization secures one mortgage for land occupied by multiple families. Pag-IBIG finances individual buyer loans.
rationale.c: Both SHFC and Pag-IBIG are subject to DHSUD oversight; neither is regulated by NHA (which is a producer).
rationale.d: CMP serves any community regardless of employment status; Pag-IBIG is mandatory for all employed workers.
rationale.correct: CMP's defining feature is community-level financing—the organization secures one mortgage for land occupied by multiple families. Pag-IBIG finances individual buyer loans.
rationale.takeaway: CMP = collective community financing; Pag-IBIG = individual buyer loans. These are structurally different models.

questions.text: The Community Mortgage Program (CMP) administered by SHFC differs from Pag-IBIG financing in that CMP finances:

options.text: Individual subdivision lot buyers at market rates, focusing on personal property acquisition
A community organization collectively to acquire land the community occupies
Government employees only through mandatory contributions, limiting access to public sector workers
Medium-rise housing projects built by NHA, targeting urban development initiatives

rationale.a: That is Pag-IBIG's function for individual buyers.
rationale.b: CMP is community-level financing. An organization (not individual buyers) secures a single mortgage to purchase land occupied by multiple households. This supports in-situ upgrading.
rationale.c: GSIS finances government employees; CMP is community-based regardless of employment status.
rationale.d: NHA builds medium-rise units; CMP finances land acquisition by communities.
rationale.correct: CMP is community-level financing. An organization (not individual buyers) secures a single mortgage to purchase land occupied by multiple households. This supports in-situ upgrading.
rationale.takeaway: CMP: community-level financing; Pag-IBIG: individual buyer financing. These serve different models.

questions.text: NHA's primary role in Philippine housing is to:

options.text: Finance end-buyer housing loans through mandatory employer contributions, which are collected monthly
Regulate and license private subdivision developers, ensuring compliance with national standards
Produce housing units for resettlement, medium-rise, and sites-and-services projects
Administer community mortgage programs for informal communities, facilitating access to affordable housing

rationale.a: ERR-PLAN-019: That is Pag-IBIG's role. NHA does not finance end-buyer loans.
rationale.b: That is DHSUD's regulatory function (formerly HLURB).
rationale.c: NHA is the primary government PRODUCER of housing. It builds resettlement projects, medium-rise housing (4–5 stories), core housing, and sites-and-services schemes.
rationale.d: SHFC administers CMP; NHA builds housing units.
rationale.correct: NHA is the primary government PRODUCER of housing. It builds resettlement projects, medium-rise housing (4–5 stories), core housing, and sites-and-services schemes.
rationale.takeaway: NHA = production/building; Pag-IBIG = finance/lending. Never confuse these roles.

questions.text: According to RA 6552, the grace period before a seller may cancel a real estate installment contract is calculated as:

options.text: 2 months for every year of installments paid
60 days total, regardless of installment duration
1 month for every year of installments paid
Variable based on the purchase price of the property

rationale.a: ERR-PLAN-014: Common error. The multiplier is 1 month/year, not 2.
rationale.b: 60 days applies to < 2-year buyers without refund rights; grace period for ≥ 2-year buyers is separate calculation.
rationale.c: RA 6552 explicitly states grace period = 1 month per year of installments paid. A 4-year buyer receives 4 months grace.
rationale.d: Grace period is based on time paid, not property price.
rationale.correct: RA 6552 explicitly states grace period = 1 month per year of installments paid. A 3-year buyer receives 3 months grace; a 4-year buyer receives 4 months grace.
rationale.takeaway: Maceda grace = 1 month × years paid. A 3-year buyer = 3 months grace before cancellation.

questions.text: A buyer has paid installments for 3 years on a subdivision lot purchased under RA 6552. The seller wants to cancel the contract due to missed payments. What is the minimum refund owed?

options.text: No refund; only a grace period applies
25% of total payments
50% of total payments
75% of total payments

rationale.a: Grace period applies to < 2 years payments only.
rationale.c: 3 years of payments exceeds the 2-year threshold. Maceda Law mandates 50% minimum refund for ≥ 2 years paid (additional 5% per year above 5 years applies here only partially).
rationale.d: 75% applies only at 5+ years with the additional 5%/year calculation.
rationale.correct: 3 years of payments exceeds the 2-year threshold. Maceda Law mandates 50% minimum refund for ≥ 2 years paid (additional 5% per year above 5 years applies here only partially).
rationale.takeaway: Maceda thresholds: < 2 yrs = grace; ≥ 2 yrs = 50% base; > 5 yrs = 50% + (5% × years beyond 5).

questions.text: Under RA 6552 (Maceda Law), a buyer who has paid installments for 1 year and 6 months then defaults. What is the seller's obligation?

options.text: Refund 50% of total payments immediately
Provide a grace period; no refund required
Refund 25% of total payments plus 2-month grace period
Provide a 6-month grace period and 25% refund

rationale.a: ERR-PLAN-013: 50% refund only applies if 2 years or more have been paid.
rationale.b: Maceda Law requires 2 years minimum installments paid before a refund is triggered. Below 2 years: grace period only (1 month per year paid = 1.5 months grace here).
rationale.c: Buyers below 2 years do not receive any refund percentage.
rationale.d: Grace period is 1 month per year (1.5 months here), not 6 months.
rationale.correct: Maceda Law requires 2 years minimum installments paid before a refund is triggered. Below 2 years: grace period only (1 month per full year of installments paid. For 1 year 6 months: typically 1 month grace (partial years may not count as full years under strict interpretation). Verify with RA 6552 Section 3 for partial-year treatment.).
rationale.takeaway: Maceda threshold: < 2 years = grace period only; ≥ 2 years = 50% minimum refund.

questions.text: A condominium buyer has paid 6 years of installments and then defaults. Under RA 6552, what refund is due if the seller cancels the contract?

options.text: 50% of total payments only, which is the minimum refund stipulated under the law for buyers who have paid at least two years of installments
50% plus 5% of total payments (55% total), reflecting the additional refund percentage for each year beyond five years of installment payments
50% plus (5% × number of years beyond 5 years) = 50% + 5% = 55% minimum
100% refund for installment periods exceeding 5 years, which is a common misunderstanding and not supported by RA 6552

rationale.a: Incomplete; the additional 5%/year for years beyond 5 years is not applied.
rationale.b: Phrasing is ambiguous. The correct statement is 50% + 5% (one additional year beyond 5).
rationale.c: Maceda: ≥ 2 years = 50% base. For > 5 years, add 5% per year beyond 5. At 6 years: 50% + (5% × 1) = 55% minimum.
rationale.d: Refunds cap at 90% total per RA 6552 Section 4 (not verified in provided search results; recommend cross-reference with full RA 6552 text).
rationale.correct: Maceda: ≥ 2 years = 50% base. For > 5 years, add 5% per year beyond 5. At 6 years: 50% + (5% × 1) = 55% minimum.
rationale.takeaway: Maceda refund formula: 50% base (≥ 2 yrs) + 5% per year beyond 5 years, capped at 90%.

questions.text: Under RA 6552, what is the PRIMARY legal distinction between a buyer who has paid fewer than 2 years of installments and a buyer who has paid 2 years or more?

options.text: The < 2-year buyer receives a longer grace period, allowing more time to settle arrears
The ≥ 2-year buyer is entitled to a refund; the < 2-year buyer receives only grace period
The < 2-year buyer must pay additional penalties; the ≥ 2-year buyer is exempt from such penalties
The ≥ 2-year buyer must accept higher interest rates on renewal, reflecting increased financial risk

rationale.a: Grace period is actually 1 month per year for both; < 2-year buyers may get proportionally less total grace (< 2 months total).
rationale.b: The 2-year threshold is the critical dividing line in Maceda Law. Below: grace period only (no refund). At or above: 50% minimum refund + grace period.
rationale.c: Maceda Law protects buyers; it does not impose penalties on < 2-year buyers.
rationale.d: Maceda Law governs installment cancellation and refunds; it does not address interest rate renewal.
rationale.correct: The 2-year threshold is the critical dividing line in Maceda Law. Below: grace period only (no refund). At or above: 50% minimum refund + grace period.
rationale.takeaway: RA 6552 threshold: 2 years paid = refund trigger. Below 2 years = grace only; ≥ 2 years = 50% refund.

questions.text: Which Philippine housing finance agency is responsible for FINANCING housing loans to employed workers?

options.text: NHA (National Housing Authority)
Pag-IBIG Fund (HDMF)
SHFC (Social Housing Finance Corporation)
DHSUD (Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development)

rationale.a: ERR-PLAN-019: NHA builds housing and manages resettlement projects; it does not finance end-buyer loans.
rationale.b: Pag-IBIG/HDMF finances housing loans for employed sector workers through mandatory contribution system. Membership is mandatory for all employees.
rationale.c: SHFC finances community-based mortgage programs (CMP), not individual buyer loans.
rationale.d: DHSUD is the regulatory body for housing developers; it does not finance loans.
rationale.correct: Pag-IBIG/HDMF finances housing loans for employed sector workers through mandatory contribution system. Membership is mandatory for employed workers (employers must register employees); self-employed and non-employed individuals may join voluntarily.
rationale.takeaway: Pag-IBIG finances individual buyer loans; NHA produces housing. These are separate roles.
